changed_reading.after: The ayah regulates how to work within an entangled verbal relation: add concretely beneficent conduct, while recognizing that rights-withholding conduct ruptures the normal reciprocal conditions.
changed_reading.before: The ayah gives a rule to debate politely, with an unexplained exception.

seeds.focus_anchor: The construction "do not dispute ... except by that which is best," followed by the exception for those who wrong.

changed_reading.after: The utterance constructs a shared revelatory relation: distinct communities receive parallel deliveries whose joined orientation is the one God.
changed_reading.before: The speaker points out that two religions have related scriptures and one deity.

seeds.focus_anchor: "People of the Book," the parallel "sent down to us / sent down to you," and "our God and your God is one."

changed_reading.after: The clause performs trusted assent, relinquishes ultimate control to God, and thereby sets a peaceable posture for the exchange.
changed_reading.before: The final clause is a doctrinal self-identification.

seeds.focus_anchor: "Say: we have believed ... and to Him we are muslimun."

changed_reading.after: The grammar distinguishes the affiliated community from members whose concrete misplacement or rights-withholding behavior changes the conditions of engagement.
changed_reading.before: The exception marks a vaguely hostile subset of the People of the Book.

seeds.focus_anchor: The repeated exception construction: "except by what is best, except those among them who wrong."

changed_reading.after: "We believe" is a publicly testable pledge whose truth must be borne out under pressure, so common-ground speech is morally costly rather than merely diplomatic.
changed_reading.before: "We believe" is a useful common formula in courteous dialogue.
